newsitem.title: UK: RALLYING-SAINZ CELEBRATES 10 YEARS AT THE TOP.
newsitem.headline: RALLYING-SAINZ CELEBRATES 10 YEARS AT THE TOP.

text.p: For Spaniard Carlos Sainz, this weekend's Rally of Portugal is a little bit special.

Not only will it give him the chance to improve on his current second place behind Scotsman Colin McRae in this year's World Championship but it also marks his 10th anniversary in the top echelons of the sport.

Like cyclist Miguel Indurain and golfer Seve Ballesteros, Sainz has become a national hero at home to the extent that, in 1994, King Juan Carlos presented him with a Gold Medal, the highest accolade which can be given to a sportsman.

That popularity will certainly give a boost to the double world champion, who won the Rally of Portugal in 1991 and 1995, as a vast horde of fans is expected to trek across the Iberian border to join in the celebrations.
"It's a rally I know and one I like," said Sainz. "I am sure a lot of Spanish people will cross the border and come and watch and give me support."
It was 10 years ago, in the 1987 Rally of Portugal, that Sainz, now 34, made an immediate mark on his world championship debut.
He stormed his Ford Sierra Cosworth into an early lead after the opening stage before retiring later with turbocharger problems.
Since then, he has emerged as one of the most successful rally stars of the past decade and one of his country's best-known sports personalities.
He has won the world championship on two occasions, with Toyota in 1990 and 1992, and has collected a total of 18 victories.
And, with the exception of 1993, he has been involved in the title race right up to, and including, the final round every year since 1991.
Perhaps that success should come as no surprise from a man who excelled in his youth at a number of sports.
At 16, he became Spain's national squash champion, and he also showed a real flair for skiing, tennis and golf.
Most impressively, his footballing prowess was rewarded with an offer of a trial from Real Madrid. He turned them down but still plays amateur soccer when he is at home in Madrid.
Soccer's loss, though, was rallying's gain as he followed in the footsteps of his older brother Antonio.
Carlos competed initially in club racing in Spain but hit the big time in 1985 when he abandoned his university studies to take up the offer of a drive in the Spanish Rally Championship with Renault.
He finished runner-up that season and did the same the next year before his switch to Ford for 1987 and his ascent to the top of his sport.
Last October, there were signs that Sainz was tiring of his sport when he suggested that the continual grind of competition might make this season his last.
But those thoughts are a long way from his mind at the moment as he concentrates on the rally this weekend.
"This rally will be a good indicator for the rest of the championship," he said.
"It's the first event of the year on gravel and the first time the team can gauge the car's performance on gravel, so I'm looking forward to it."

Second places in Monte Carlo and Sweden and a retirement on the Safari event have taken him to second and there is little doubt that he wants to improve that position on the rally which made his name 10 years ago.
